title: Adult Learning Principles for GIS Instruction: Lessons Learned from Teaching Wildland Fire Professionals
presenter: Heather Heward (Forest, Rangeland and Fire Sciences, University of Idaho)
description_full:
You may be a GIS wizard in map production, sharing, and collaboration, but how do you handle a classroom of students facing countless error messages from self-inflicted or program-related issues, or even a lab mate who sucks up your work time with their GIS problems? Your ability to share your knowledge about GIS while fostering a growth mindset for the people you work with is the real mark of a GIS master. Hear my lessons learned from decades of teaching wildland fire professional GIS, and have an interactive discussion on how to use adult learning principles to maximize your effectiveness as a teacher of GIS and prepare the next generation of GIS teachers.

##### Bio 

Heather Heward is director of the Student of Fire Initiative and a Research Assistant Professor in Forest, Rangeland, and Fire Sciences who investigates wildland fire behavior and training design. Her recent work examines how federal prescribed fire training can be improved using adult learning principles. She has also studied the relationship between fire intensity and burn severity using satellite remote sensing data from western U.S. fires.

title: Better Understanding Wildfire with Spatial Data: Pre-fire, Post-fire, and Past-fires
presenter: Keith T. Weber (GIS Director, Idaho State University)
description_full:
This presentation will discuss how spatial data and GIS can be used to model fire susceptibility, hazard, risk, and conflagration risk using GIS and satellite remote sensing capabilities. The resulting models can be used to inform decision-makers and enable science-driven pre-fire mitigation planning. We will also look at the RECOVER post-fire decision support platform and its ability to help manage and monitor the post-fire landscape. Lastly, we will dive into the Historic Fires Database to better understand the broader wildfire landscape and burn-on-burn events.

title: Short Talks - Morning
presenter: Ashton Sellke (Plant Sciences, University of Idaho); Shashwot Niraula (WSP USA); Daniel Cronan (School of Design and Construction, Washington State University); Jennifer Ladino, Erin James, Megan Davis, Antonio Isiordia (Confluence Lab, University of Idaho)
description: Ten minute presentations highlighting recent geospatial-related work
description_full:
Presenters from across the geospatial, GIS, and drone community will give 10-minute presentations highlighting their recent work.

##### Presentations

- Ashton Sellke (Plant Sciences, University of Idaho) - **Predicting Turkish Thistle (Carduus cinereus) Habitat Through Susceptibility Modeling in Canyon Grasslands of Oregon and Idaho** - Environmental variables that influence the spatial distributions of plant species can be combined with presence data in a GIS to predict areas of susceptible habitat for Turkish thistle. A habitat susceptibility model should decrease survey inputs and determine effort needed for control across a landscape with considerable challenges to safe accessibility.
- Shashwot Niraula (WSP USA) - **Geospatial Application Developer** - This talk demos a custom roadway video viewer built in ArcGIS Experience Builder, which syncs road video with a map so users can explore assets and conditions along a route. I'll also show how AI tools like computer vision and large language models can work with GIS and modern software development to automate tasks and make geospatial data easier to use.
- Daniel Cronan (School of Design and Construction, Washington State University) - **From GIS to GeoAI: Teaching Students to Map, Model, and Design Future Landscapes** - This talk explores how GIS can be taught as more than a mapping tool by integrating spatial analysis, scenario planning, and emerging GeoAI methods into graduate and design education. Drawing from a graduate NSF NRT course and a landscape architecture studio, I will share approaches for helping students move from understanding existing landscape conditions to modeling future change, evaluating alternative scenarios, and using geospatial data to inform design and planning decisions.
- Jennifer Ladino, Erin James, Megan Davis, Antonio Isiordia (Confluence Lab, University of Idaho) - **Mapping Fire Stories: A Confluence Lab Project** - Data visualizations of wildfire, while helpful for spreading information, often limit fire to a discrete event and flatten out our embodied emotional experiences of fire and smoke. By inviting users to map and share stories of fire along personal timelines and emotional registers, the Confluence Lab's fire postcards expand what counts as a fire map--beyond the familiar imagery of flames, AQI smoke maps, and outlines of burn scars or devastated neighborhoods. Our interactive postcards show how individual wildfire experiences overlap or contradict each other, opening new ways of relating to our neighbors and to our changing landscape by amplifying stories that were previously unheard or simplified. Come learn about this ongoing project and map your story of fire!

title: Remotely Sensed Data in Natural Resources
presenter: Jason Karl (Director of the Rangeland Center, Rangeland Ecology, University of Idaho); Ed Flathers (College of Natural Resources Forest Innovations Institute, University of Idaho); Bruce Ripley (Chief innovation officer, College of Natural Resources, University of Idaho)
description_full:
Remote sensed data in natural resource comes in many forms. This session will focus on how some of the more advanced remote sensing techniques such as gaussian splatting are transforming data collection, how those images are transformed into not just an immersive 3D environment but a complete high resolution 3D dataset that can be geolocated with other GIS information to make a complete high resolution digital twin of your study area.

Individual talks:

- Dr. Jason Karl - Collection of high resolution imagery and transformation into a gaussian splat.
- Dr. Ed Flathers - High precision georeferencing of unregistered drone information, co-registering those data with high precision LiDAR point clouds and transformation into a single product.
- Bruce Ripley - How we put high resolution remote sensed data to use in the applied world to make decisions and how a digital forest twin is much more than a collection of trees.
